{"representations":[{"case_ref":"sample_9b3ff859d9bec486","text":"Your March 30–April 12 records are mostly steady compared with your preceding 28 days. RMSSD fell to 23 ms on April 5, versus your baseline range of 43–47, then returned to 43–46 for all seven remaining days. This isolated dip lowered the average to 43.1 from 45.3 ms; the median stayed 45. The lower weekend average mainly reflects that one Sunday, rather than a repeated weekend pattern. Sleep, movement and resting heart rate showed no matching unusual change that day.

Sleep averaged 7h48 versus 7h51, with bedtime about three minutes later and waking fixed at 07:00. Steps averaged 7,954 versus 8,066; active time stayed near 55 minutes and low movement near 453 versus 451 minutes, mainly between 10:00 and 18:30. Resting heart rate edged down to 55.8 from 56.3 bpm. Activity remained around 21:00, with essentially no relationship to following-night sleep duration. No values were missing. Watch whether the isolated RMSSD dip recurs."},{"case_ref":"sample_57f611dd4b2ab003","text":"Your resting heart rate shows a sustained change: it moved from 51–53 bpm throughout your 28-day baseline to 61–63 on every day of March 30–April 12. The average rose from 51.8 to 61.7 bpm, about 9.9 bpm or 19%. This appeared immediately, persisted across weekdays and weekends, and had not returned by the final day.

Other measurements stayed close to your baseline: RMSSD averaged 45.1 versus 44.8 ms, and sleep 7h52 versus 7h51, with bedtime near 22:48 and waking consistently at 07:00. Steps averaged 7,923 versus 7,938, although they trended downward within the window. Active time increased slightly to 56.2 from 54.7 minutes; low movement decreased to 447 from 450 minutes. Activity remained at 21:00 and had little relationship to following-night sleep duration. Heart rate and RMSSD were only weakly related within the window. All measurements were present. Continued recording can show whether the heart-rate shift persists; these records do not explain it."},{"case_ref":"sample_6eec85b3c4f2fb93","text":"Your sleep changed sharply halfway through March 30–April 12. The first seven nights remained near your 28-day baseline of 8h01, at 7h54–8h05. Sleep ending April 6–12 then fell to 5h57–6h08 on seven consecutive nights, without returning. Sleep starts shifted from roughly 22:39 to 00:32–00:43, while waking stayed at 07:00. The full-window average of 7h02, down 59 minutes, therefore understates the final week's reduction. Both weekdays and weekends were affected.

Movement and heart measurements showed no comparable shift: steps averaged 7,979 versus 7,976, active time 54.4 versus 55.5 minutes, low movement about 450 in both periods, and resting heart rate 56.2 versus 56.1 bpm. RMSSD averaged 44.2 versus 45.3 ms and remained within your baseline range. Activity stayed around 21:00; its relationship with following-night sleep duration was weak (r = −0.26), providing no causal explanation. No values were missing. Track whether the later sleep timing continues."},{"case_ref":"sample_61018e0de4ab948a","text":"Your sleep duration increased slightly, but its timing became much more variable. Across March 30–April 12, sleep alternated nightly between starts at 22:07–22:16 with 06:30 waking, and starts at 00:37–00:44 with 09:00 waking. This persisted through both weeks and across weekdays and weekends. Your baseline had starts around 22:50 and fixed 07:00 waking. Consecutive wake times now differed by 2h30, despite sleep duration remaining steady at 7h54–8h03. Average sleep rose to 7h58 from 7h50, with no meaningful within-window duration trend.

Steps increased slightly to 8,052 from 7,940 and trended upward. Active time averaged 52.7 versus 54.4 minutes, rising during the window and higher on weekends; low movement averaged 449 versus 452 minutes. Resting heart rate and RMSSD remained within baseline ranges, averaging 56.4 bpm and 45 ms. Activity stayed near 21:00, with little relationship to following-night sleep duration. No values were missing. Recording sleep timing alongside duration would capture the persistent alternation."}]}
